wait_time: up to 7 days (Apple emails you when it is ready)
format: one or more .zip files, split into chunks you choose (1-25 GB each)

steps.title: Sign in at privacy.apple.com
steps.detail: Use the same Apple ID whose data you want. This is the official GDPR / data-portability portal, separate from iCloud.

steps.title: Choose "Get a copy of your data"
steps.detail: Then "Get started" under Obtain a copy of your data.

steps.title: Select what to include
steps.detail: Tick the categories you want. iCloud Photos is the large one, and it is listed separately from the account information - your sign-in records, purchases and app history are their own entries and are small by comparison. If you only want the photographs, take only that; if this is a once-and-for-all copy, take everything, since the wait is the same.

steps.title: Pick a maximum file size
steps.detail: Apple splits the export into chunks and lets you choose how big they are, from 1 GB up to 25 GB. Pick the largest your disk and your connection will tolerate: a 20 GB library at the 5 GB setting arrives as four files, and at 1 GB as twenty. Fewer, larger files means fewer downloads to shepherd and fewer chances for one to fail partway.

steps.title: Submit and wait
steps.detail: Apple verifies the request and prepares the export, which takes up to seven days - the longest wait of any of the big services. There is no progress to watch and no way to hurry it. Make the request before you need it rather than the evening you have set aside to sort your photographs.

steps.title: Download every part
steps.detail: Download all the numbered parts and keep them in one folder. The links expire after a few days; let them lapse and the whole seven-day wait starts again. Do not unzip them - Muletto reads the archives directly, which saves both the time and the doubled disk space.

steps.title: Open the parts together
steps.detail: Drop every part into Muletto at once. It reads them as one export, decodes the HEIC without converting anything, puts the dates and locations back into the files themselves, and finds the photographs that also exist in your Google or Snapchat archives. If you want ordinary JPEGs at the end, there is a box for that when you save.

notes: What this export does not contain, which catches nearly everybody: no passwords. Those are end-to-end encrypted in iCloud, so Apple holds them as blobs it has no key for. Health is less clear-cut and worth knowing about: Apple's own support pages say health data can come as part of a data request, but a real eighteen-archive export requested in July 2026 arrived with none in it. Tick it if it is offered, and get it off the phone as well - that takes a minute and definitely works. Health comes off the iPhone instead, in about a minute - there is a separate Apple Health guide here for it. Photographs are a different case: not secret, just large, so they are their own item to select rather than part of the account archives. And if you have Advanced Data Protection switched on, the encrypted set grows to around twenty-three categories, so your export gets smaller rather than larger.
This export gives you full-resolution originals, not the compressed previews some sync tools leave behind.
Download links expire after a few days, so save every part promptly.
A large library arrives as several multi-gigabyte files. Keep them together in one folder and open them together.

Apple also offers a separate service that transfers your iCloud Photos collection directly to another provider. That is a different thing from this export: it moves your library to another company rather than giving you a copy of your own.

HEIC files keep working after Muletto writes dates and locations back, and export as they came unless you ask for JPEG on the way out - one box on the save screen, converted here rather than uploaded anywhere, at roughly double the file size.

muletto_support.status: reads the nested archives, photos, messages and the health export. Measured on a real 18-archive export

explain.title: Your iPhone photographs come back as HEIC, and most tools will not open them
explain.body: Apple hands your files back in their original format, which for anything shot on a recent iPhone means HEIC rather than JPEG. That is the honest thing to do and it is also why an Apple export so often looks broken: Windows shows grey placeholders, plenty of photo tools refuse it outright, and the usual advice is to convert everything first. Muletto reads HEIC directly, using the same video codec your browser already has, so there is no conversion step before you can see what you were sent. When you save your library back out you choose: keep them as they came, or tick one box and have them written as JPEG. The conversion happens on your own machine, it keeps the date and the place, and it is worth knowing that a JPEG is the only one of the two a capture date can be written into - so converting is also what lets a repaired date travel with the file.

faq.q: Why did Apple send me eighteen separate zip files?
faq.a: Apple sends one archive per category, and splits anything larger than the size limit you picked when requesting. Several of those archives contain further zip files inside them, so a single category can be two levels deep.

faq.q: How long does an Apple data request take?
faq.a: Apple says up to seven days and it is often less. Once ready, the download stays available for about two weeks, after which the request has to be made again.

faq.q: Why are there no photos in my Apple privacy export?
faq.a: iCloud Photos is a separate category and has to be selected when the request is made. If it was included it arrives as its own set of archives, which for a large library can be very big.

faq.q: What is inside the Apple Media Services archive?
faq.a: Purchase history, App Store activity, Apple Music listening and Game Center data. It holds further zip files rather than plain spreadsheets, so anything that unpacks only one level will appear to find almost nothing in it.
